# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The expansion of transcatheter therapies for structural heart disease has created an urgent need for reliable large-bore vascular access in patients with prohibitive peripheral arterial anatomy. While transfemoral access remains the default route for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), up to 15% of candidates have iliofemoral disease, small caliber vessels, or heavy calcification that preclude safe transfemoral delivery [1,2]. Alternative routes—transapical, transaortic, subclavian, and transcarotid—each carry distinct morbidity profiles [3,4]. Transcaval access, in which a sheath is advanced from the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the abdominal aorta through a deliberately created aortocaval tract, has emerged as a fully percutaneous alternative that avoids surgical incisions and thoracic morbidity [5,6].

## Technique and Physiological Rationale

The transcaval technique exploits the high retroperitoneal pressure surrounding the infrarenal aorta, which limits bleeding even when a large hole is created, provided the patient is not coagulopathic [5]. Under fluoroscopic and often fusion-imaging guidance, an electrified guidewire is directed from a catheter in the IVC across to a target snare or marker in the aorta [6,7]. Electrosurgical energy applied to the back end of a 0.014-inch wire enables tissue traversal, after which the large-bore sheath is advanced over a stiff wire into the aorta [7,8]. At procedure end, the residual aortocaval tract is closed using a nitinol cardiac occluder device, permitting controlled hemostasis with persistent—and usually clinically benign—aortocaval flow [9,10].

Careful preprocedural computed tomography planning is essential to select a crossing target free of aortic calcification or interposed bowel and to confirm an adequate aortocaval window [11,12]. Calcium-free aortic segments are preferentially targeted to facilitate both crossing and closure [12].

## Clinical Evidence

The first-in-human report by Greenbaum and colleagues established feasibility in patients with no other transcatheter option [6]. The prospective multicenter Transcaval Access study subsequently demonstrated a high procedural success rate (99%) with acceptable safety, reporting successful transcaval crossing and device delivery in the large majority of enrolled patients undergoing TAVR [13]. Registry data have confirmed favorable 30-day survival comparable to other non-femoral approaches [14,15].

Comparative analyses suggest that transcaval access yields outcomes at least equivalent to transthoracic alternatives while reducing length of stay and avoiding the respiratory complications associated with transapical and transaortic routes [16,17]. Vascular and bleeding complications, though present, are frequently manageable percutaneously [18]. Importantly, retroperitoneal bleeding and aortocaval fistula persistence remain the principal concerns, with most fistulas closing spontaneously or remaining hemodynamically insignificant over time [19,20].

Beyond TAVR, transcaval access has been applied to mechanical circulatory support device delivery, endovascular aneurysm repair adjuncts, and emerging transcatheter mitral and tricuspid platforms requiring large delivery systems [21,22]. Its versatility has positioned it as a general-purpose large-bore access strategy [23].

## Complications and Management

The dominant complication is bleeding into the retroperitoneum, which can require transfusion, covered stent placement, or, rarely, surgical or endovascular rescue [18,24]. Series have documented that most bleeding events are controlled with prolonged occluder tamponade or adjunctive endovascular maneuvers [24,25]. Device embolization and incomplete closure are infrequent but reported [25]. Renal protection through judicious contrast use and meticulous CT-based targeting reduces both crossing failure and adjacent organ injury [11,26].

Long-term follow-up demonstrates that persistent aortocaval fistulas are usually small and well tolerated, although high-output flow occasionally necessitates secondary closure [19,27]. Dedicated closure devices designed specifically for the aortocaval tract are under investigation and may further reduce bleeding [28].

## Future Directions

Refinements in imaging fusion, dedicated crossing and closure hardware, and operator training are expected to broaden adoption [26,28]. As transcatheter therapies for mitral and tricuspid disease mature and demand ever-larger sheaths, transcaval access may assume a more central role in the structural heart toolkit [22,29]. Standardized training pathways and multicenter outcome registries will be critical to defining its appropriate place among alternative access strategies [29,30].

## Conclusion

Transcaval access offers a fully percutaneous, surgically sparing solution for patients requiring large-bore arterial access who lack adequate transfemoral anatomy. Supported by growing prospective and registry evidence, it achieves high procedural success with a complication profile that compares favorably with transthoracic approaches [13,16,30]. With continued technical refinement and dedicated closure technology, transcaval access is poised to become an increasingly important component of structural heart intervention.
